claims.statement: The `sources` argument to `align_citations` accepts three forms that are normalized into the same internal candidate list: plain `str`, `SourceDocument`, and `SourceChunk`. Mixing them in one call is allowed.
`SourceDocument(id, text, metadata=...)` is a full document; its `id` becomes the `source_id` on every `Citation` and `RetrievalSupport` that resolves to that document.

`SourceChunk(source_id, text, doc_char_start, doc_char_end)` is a pre-chunked excerpt. Internally, alignment runs against the chunk text; the chunk's `doc_char_start` is added to the resulting offsets so that `source.text[citation.char_start:citation.char_end] == citation.evidence` still holds with offsets absolute in the parent document. `SourceChunk` validates this slice when `document_text` is provided at construction time.

Each `SpanCitations` returned by `align_citations` has exactly four fields: `answer_span` (an `AnswerSpan` with text and `char_start`/`char_end` in the answer), `citations` (a list of `Citation` ranked best first, may be empty), `retrieval_support` (a list of `RetrievalSupport`), and `status` (one of `"supported"`, `"partial"`, `"unsupported"`).

Status is driven by the best exact `Citation`'s `answer_coverage` and the cheap contradiction check, not by embedding similarity. A high embedding score that never localizes is a `RetrievalSupport`, not a `Citation`, and does not flip the status.

`"supported"` means the top citation's `answer_coverage >= supported_answer_coverage` (default 0.6) and contradiction did not fire. `"partial"` means citations exist but coverage is below the threshold, or contradiction fired. `"unsupported"` means no citation survived filtering. The literal is `"partial"`, never `"partially_supported"`. Contradiction downgrades to `"partial"`, not `"unsupported"`.
The `SpanCitations` model validator enforces that `"unsupported"` requires an empty `citations` list, and that `"supported"` or `"partial"` requires at least one citation.

All character offsets (`AnswerSpan`, `Citation`, `EvidenceSpan`) are Python half-open intervals: `char_start` inclusive, `char_end` exclusive, and `text[char_start:char_end]` is the slice the offset pair refers to. The evidence equality invariant — `source.text[citation.char_start:citation.char_end] == citation.evidence` after chunk rebasing — is what makes the offsets safe to feed directly to a Python slicer.

On the default / Rust path, prepare builds an inverted index over source passage windows and rare-token intersect chooses which windows get Smith-Waterman. Smith-Waterman still localizes the citation; the index only chooses the windows. If the Rust extension is missing, or a custom tokenizer or segmenter is supplied, `PreparedCitationCorpus.from_sources` leaves `inverted_index=None` and `_select_candidates` falls back to lexical selection.

When an embedder is provided, `_add_embedding_candidates` can add non-index windows to the candidate set; those extras still need Smith-Waterman to produce a `Citation`. Rust prepare still runs with an embedder when `SimpleTokenizer` and `SimpleSegmenter` are in use, and the embedding index is built on the prepared candidates. `retrieval_support` is not a `Citation` and does not flip status.

Content-word overlap on the candidate passage can emit a citation when sequential Smith-Waterman coverage is low, so grounded how-to and news paraphrases are not dropped to `"unsupported"` for reordered content words. Structured field:value sources (Data2txt hours, amenities) get a second Smith-Waterman pass with `gap_score=0`; faithful rewrites of known fields can land on `"supported"` or `"partial"`, invented fields stay `"unsupported"`. Both paths still require an exact localized evidence slice and do not produce embedding-only citations.

A custom tokenizer or segmenter disables the Rust inverted-index fast path: `from_sources` leaves `inverted_index=None` and candidate selection falls back to lexical prefilter, but Smith-Waterman still runs on whatever the fallback selects.
